# Task 26: Chapter cover, chapter-end card, and Chapter in panels

Repo martinmw13/LectorIA-meta. Work on the existing branch `chapter-panels` (built on `folio-reader`, task 16, the Folio reader) in the worktree /workspace/wt-26. Read AGENTS.md, docs/contracts.md, docs/tasks/16-folio-reader.md and app/leer/*, app/folio/* first. The prototype is /workspace/wt-26/.proto/03-folio-margin.html (panels tile, panels modal, recap) and .proto/01-folio-carousel.html (paired "Picture scene / Picture chapter" pane control). Port the look, not the code.

## Hard constraints
- Do not modify core/music-* logic, the Player audio logic, or anything under server/images.
- No image generation of any kind, no network calls to image or music providers. Panels use bundled art or placeholders only.
- Never run `next start` or `next dev`. Run tests, typecheck and build only.
- English UI, Meta blue accents only (never purple), desktop only, minimalist.
- No scene names anywhere (no scene titles in the UI). The word "Generated" never appears in user-facing copy.
- The phrase "Chapter in panels" appears exactly ONCE on any screen (never a heading plus the same words in a card).
- Music changes only at scene change: the cover and end page belong to scenes, so they never trigger a music change of their own.
- Keep repo rules: small focused commits, RESCUE_LOG.md if you rescue anything, file-size hook, secrets scan.

## 1. Chapter cover (page 0 of each chapter's first scene)
- The first scene of every chapter gets one extra leading sub-page: the cover. Its text pages shift by one. Do this with a pure core helper (e.g. `subPageCount(sceneId, paragraphsPages, isChapterFirst)` or a `withCovers(views, model)` in core/reader.ts) used by both the route (page counts for navReducer) and ScenePage, with tests: cover is index 0, `enterAtEnd` lands on the real last page, Back from text page 1 returns to the cover, Back from the cover goes to the previous chapter's last page.
- Cover layout in the reading column: kicker "Chapter", a very large number (Newsreader, light, e.g. 7–8rem, the chapter number from parsed data, digits), the chapter title large below it, a thin rule, then the panels offer card, then a primary "Begin the chapter →" button (moves to the next sub-page; ArrowRight works as usual). No "Scene k of n" line and no drop cap on the cover.
- The panels offer card on the cover is spoiler-gated: a row of the chapter's panel thumbnails rendered heavily blurred (filter: blur(10px) saturate(.7), pointer-events none, aria-hidden), with a small eye-off icon, the name "Chapter in panels" once, the line "The whole chapter, told in pictures. It gives away what happens, so you may want to read first.", and two buttons: "Show me anyway" (opens the panels view) and "I'll read first" (collapses the card to a one-line quiet link "Chapter in panels" for this chapter in this session). Prominent but calm: generous size, hairline border, paper background.
- Left image pane on the cover: the paper-grain placeholder with no pill (nothing to picture yet).

## 2. Chapter-end page (trailing sub-page of each chapter's last scene)
- The last scene of every chapter gets one extra trailing sub-page: the chapter end. Same pure helper, tests included.
- Layout: kicker "End of Chapter N", a large card "Relive this chapter in panels" with an UNBLURRED preview strip of the first 3–4 panels (no spoiler risk now), a primary "Open the panels" button, then a quiet "On to Chapter N+1 →" button that goes to the next chapter's cover. Last chapter: "The end." in place of the next link.
- The phrase "Chapter in panels" must not also appear on this page (the card title already says it).

## 3. Panels view
- A modal dialog (role=dialog, aria-modal, aria-label with the chapter title, e.g. "Chapter 1, The Cyclone"), opened from the cover, the end page, or the pane control. Escape and a × button close it; focus returns to the opener; focus is trapped while open.
- Header: "Chapter 1 · The Cyclone" in small caps style, nothing else.
- One panel per scene of the chapter, in order, laid out like a comic page: CSS grid, 3 columns (2 for chapters with ≤4 scenes), 2–3 px ink borders, small gutters, the first panel of each row may span 2 columns for rhythm. The grid scrolls inside the dialog if needed; the dialog fits 1280x800.
- Panel art, in this priority: (a) the scene picture already in the session cache from "Picture this scene" (app/folio/use-pictures.ts `sceneCache`; export a read-only getter, don't change its behaviour); (b) bundled art from a static map `PANEL_ART` in app/folio/panels.ts: c1s2 → /art/panels/cyclone-doorway.jpg, c1s3 → /art/panels/cyclone-house.jpg; (c) a placeholder: paper background with a faint diagonal ink hatch and a tiny pencil glyph, no text label.
- Caption box under or over each panel (cream box, italic serif, small): a short caption from a pure helper `panelCaption(summary)` in core: first clause/sentence of the scene summary, cut at a word boundary to ≤ 90 chars with "…". Test it.
- NO numbered circles. Each panel shows only a tiny faint number (9px, 35% opacity of muted text) in its top-left corner, visible only on hover/focus-within.
- Click a panel with art: open the shared Lightbox. Placeholders are not clickable.
- Data: the route passes the current chapter's panels only (sceneId + caption + art url), built server-side. This deliberately relaxes "the client never receives other scenes' summaries": record in docs/contracts-chapters.md that the client receives the current chapter's short panel captions only, shown behind the spoiler gate, and never other chapters' or full summaries.

## 4. Pane control on other scenes
- On every text page (not the cover, not the end page) the image pane's pill becomes a paired control, one rounded pill with two halves: "Picture this scene" | "Picture the chapter". The left half is the existing scene picture action. The right half opens the panels view; if the reader has not reached this chapter's end page in this session and has not chosen "Show me anyway" for this chapter, it first opens a small spoiler gate dialog: line "The whole chapter, told in pictures. It gives away what happens, so you may want to read first." with "Show me anyway" / "Not yet". (The dialog does not repeat "Chapter in panels".)
- When a scene picture is showing, keep the existing image behaviour (hover expand, lightbox) and put a small quiet "Picture the chapter" text button under the image.

## 5. Copy and docs
- Every new string must be warm, short and plain. Collect every new user-facing string in docs/tasks/26-chapter-panels.md as a table.
- Record the cover/end sub-pages and the panels data in docs/contracts-chapters.md.
- grep gates: no "Generated" in app/ or core/ user strings; no purple hex; "Chapter in panels" occurs once per screen (write a unit test or a simple grep check over the components that render on the same screen).

## Finish
Run npm test, npx next typegen, npm run typecheck, npm run build, npm run check:isolation, npm run test:hooks, npm run check:size, the secrets scan. Commit. No push. End with a short summary of what you did, what you skipped, and risks.

## Docs size note
docs/contracts.md is at the 20000-byte pre-commit cap, and another task is editing it in parallel. Do NOT edit docs/contracts.md. Put every contract change from this task (cover/end sub-pages, panels data, the relaxed summaries rule) in a new file docs/contracts-chapters.md, written as the authoritative addendum that overrides the matching lines in contracts.md.

3|# Ponytail
4|
5|You are a lazy senior developer. The best code is the code never written. You solve the whole problem with the least new code. End your reply with one or two lines: what you skipped or did not check, and any risk the user must know.
6|
7|Active for the whole session until the user says "stop ponytail" or "normal mode". Switch level: `/ponytail lite|full|ultra`.
8|
9|## Before you write
10|
11|Read the task and the code it touches. List every place your change must reach: callers, tests, fixtures, config, exports. Check what your change could break for users: data it would destroy or expose, callers that stop working. That is scope. Extra features are not.
12|
13|## The smallest complete change
14|
15|Take the first option that fully works:
16|
17|1. Does it need to exist? Skip features, options and flexibility nobody asked for, and name them in one line. A vague request ("build me X") gets the smallest version that does the core job.
18|2. Already in this codebase (a helper, component, service, pattern)? Use it the way the surrounding code does.
19|3. Standard library or a platform feature? Use it, unless the project has its own. A house component beats a native widget.
20|4. An installed dependency? Use it. Never add a dependency for a few lines.
21|5. Can it be one line a reader gets at a glance? One line.
22|6. Otherwise: the minimum code that works.
23|
24|- Be lazy about the solution, never about the change itself: finish every part the task needs, including the callers, tests and fixtures your change breaks.
25|- No abstraction, wrapper, type conversion, option, config, boilerplate or "for later" code nobody asked for. Keep values in the form the platform already gives you. Deletion beats addition. Keep the structure the codebase already has: its layers, interfaces and conventions.
26|- The shortest working diff wins, once you know everything it must touch. A one-liner that needs decoding is not short.
27|- Comment only the why the code cannot show, in one line.
28|- Bug fix: before you edit, grep every caller of the function you touch, then fix the root cause once in the shared code.
29|- Code you move or merge keeps its error handling and validation.
30|- Between options of equal size, take the one that is correct on edge cases.
31|- Lazy code without its check is unfinished: new non-trivial logic (a branch, a loop, a parser, money or security, or a whole new script or app) leaves one small test or an assert-based self-check. Trivial changes need none.
32|- A shortcut with a known limit gets a code comment in this form: `shortcut: <the limit>, <when to upgrade>`.
33|
34|Never cut: validation at trust boundaries, error handling that prevents data loss, security, accessibility, the calibration real hardware needs, anything the user asked for.
35|
36|## Levels
37|
38|| Level | Behavior |
39||-------|----------|
40|| **lite** | Build what was asked. Name the smaller option in one line and let the user pick. |
41|| **full** | The rules above. Default. |
42|| **ultra** | Also question the request: before building, push back on any part the need does not justify. |
43|
44|Run `ponytail-review` on your own diff before you hand it back.

46|## Skills
47|
48|All pstack and ponytail skills live in `.agents/skills/`. Muse Code loads them when the workspace starts with `--trust-workspace`. Most pstack skills are user-invocable-only, so a prompt must name the skill for it to apply.
49|
50|| Situation | Skill |
51||-----------|-------|
52|| Designing a task | `architect` |
53|| Before writing logic | `principle-foundational-thinking`, `principle-type-system-discipline` |
54|| Writing TypeScript | `typescript-best-practices` |
55|| A bug with a cheap test | `tdd` |
56|| Debugging | `principle-fix-root-causes` |
57|| Finishing a task | `principle-prove-it-works` |
58|| Reviewing | `ponytail-review`, `interrogate`, `blast-radius` |
59|| Any prose: docs, UI copy, commit messages | `unslop`, `technical-writing` |
60|
61|If no row fits, read `.agents/skills/poteto-help/SKILL.md`, which maps situations to skills.
62|
63|`interrogate` is written for Cursor. Under Muse, run the same review with Muse subagents and `muse-spark-1.3` as reviewers.
64|
65|## Workflow
66|
67|Each task follows the same loop. Muse Spark 1.3 Standard (`muse-spark-1.3`) writes the design in `docs/tasks/NN-name.md` and the review in `docs/reviews/NN.md`. `muse-spark-1.3-contributor` implements. Implement and review run at most two rounds.
68|
69|A rescue by another tool happens only after those rounds. Log it in `RESCUE_LOG.md` with the date, the task, the tool, why Muse got stuck, what changed, and the commits. Rescue commits carry a `Rescue: <tool>` trailer and no Muse Code trailer; the hook skips them.
70|
71|Save every Muse Code session transcript as JSONL in `agent-logs/NN-<step>.jsonl`. Every commit carries the Muse Code co-author trailer, which the `prepare-commit-msg` hook adds. Update `BUILT_DURING_HACKATHON.md` with each task.
72|
73|## Lectoria rules
74|
75|- The text unit is the scene, not the paragraph or chapter.
76|- Paragraph ids are global, like `c12p34`.
77|- The emotion taxonomy has 8 ASCII ids: calma, alegria, tristeza, suspenso, misterio, aventura, combate, asombro. Jev returning `unknown` counts as low confidence and goes to the Muse override, which may return only the 8 ids. A hard failure stores no vector and the scene keeps the previous track. Never fake an emotion.
78|- Jev runs at `POST https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone` with the model pinned to `jev-1.14.0`.
79|- Public-domain books only.
80|- Images follow the book text and the W. W. Denslow 1900 illustrations: silver shoes, nothing from the 1939 MGM film.
81|- Never copy code from github.com/martinmw13/lectoria.
82|- Test with the cheapest models (Contributor). Use Standard for the final pass and the public chat.
83|
84|## Product rules
85|
86|Owner decisions. Short and binding.
87|
88|- Desktop first. No mobile or iOS work now.
89|- The reader shows one scene at a time. Sub-pages split long scenes by length only. Music cues run on scene entry.
90|- A chapter holds several scenes. Each scene has its own emotion.
91|- Paragraph ids carry a global ordinal `n`. Compare `n`, never id strings.
92|- `book.json` is frozen with a `textVersion` hash. Every cache key includes it.
93|- Scenes cover each chapter's paragraphs with no gaps and no overlaps. No scene crosses a chapter boundary. Scenes split at strong sequential emotion shifts; blends stay in the vector.
94|- Emotions are distributions. Each scene stores the full Jev probability vector over the 8 ids, plus `intensity` (0 to 1) and `tempo` (energy, 0 to 1). The Muse override on low confidence edits the vector and records that it did. It never swaps in a single label.
95|- Music is about 15 tracks, pre-generated offline with MusicGen on Modal as one coherent soundtrack: same orchestra and instrumentation, same leitmotif style. Each track is a weighted blend of emotions and carries an emotion vector plus intensity and tempo. The proposed way to pick the blends: cluster the Oz scene vectors and use the centroids as track prompts.
96|- The player picks the track nearest to the scene vector, by cosine similarity over the vector plus intensity and tempo. Hysteresis stops it from flipping on small changes. Skip or change track overrides until the next scene.
97|- The owner listens to short clips before any full generation. Agents do not run Modal until the owner says so.
98|- MusicGen weights are CC-BY-NC. The hackathon demo is non-commercial. The generated tracks must say so in their README.
99|- Chat is low priority and simple. The context is the book text up to the reader's current position. The book prefix goes first and the question goes last, so readers share the prompt cache. Oz is about 55k tokens.
100|- The chat system prompt answers only from the provided text. It refuses knowledge beyond it, even if the model knows the book.
101|- A spoiler mode toggle is for readers who finished the book. It sends the whole text so they can ask about later events. No live Glimmer spoiler guard. No per-chapter summaries for chat. Citing passages is optional.
102|- Glimmer (open weights) keeps a pipeline role. Current decision: it writes the per-scene "why this music" explanation shown in the Developer View.
103|- Spikes come before feature code. Throwaway scripts in `scripts/spikes/` measure Muse Image (response format, latency, Denslow-style prompt), Meta `json_schema` structured output, and the Jev vector on a few Oz scenes. Results go to `docs/spikes.md`.
104|- Spend is counted in integer micro-dollars. Reserve with Redis `INCRBY` before each model call and refund with `DECRBY` after. Reserve per call, including retries.
105|- The server clamps every model tool argument. Tool arguments are untrusted input.
106|- The CSP allows `challenges.cloudflare.com` (script and frame) and `*.public.blob.vercel-storage.com` (images).
107|- The "Picture this" cache key is the book plus the paragraph where the selection starts plus `textVersion` plus `promptVersion`. Never generate the same image twice for one paragraph. The prompt is built from that paragraph plus scene context.
108|- The "Picture scene" cache key is the book plus the scene id plus `textVersion` plus `promptVersion`.
109|- Images live in Vercel Blob at deterministic public paths (`addRandomSuffix: false`, `allowOverwrite: false`). An index in Upstash Redis maps key to Blob URL so hits are one Redis GET; on an index miss check the Blob path with `head()` before generating and backfill the index. Routes return Blob URLs, never image bytes.
110|- Modal endpoints require proxy auth. Tokens live only in env.
111|
112|## Security rules
113|
114|Summary. The full rules live in [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md).
115|
116|- Secrets live only in env vars: `.env.local` locally (gitignored), Vercel env vars in prod.
117|- `.env.example` holds names only, never values.
118|- Never use a `NEXT_PUBLIC_` variable for a secret. Only public ids such as the Turnstile site key may use it.
119|- `core/` stays pure: no keys, no env reads, no network clients, no `server-only`. Key-holding clients live in `server/` (Next.js only, each file starts with `import 'server-only'`) and in `pipeline/` (Node scripts that read env). Callers inject them into `core` functions as arguments. Tests run `core` with fake clients.
120|- The pre-commit secret scan must pass. Never bypass it with `--no-verify`.
121|- Errors to the client are generic. Details go to server logs only, never with keys.
122|- Never log request headers.
123|
124|## Writing rules
125|
126|Run docs, UI copy, and commit messages through the `unslop` skill: no filler, no hype, no emoji in headings, none of seamless, elevate, delve, robust, leverage. Headings use sentence case. Commit messages use an imperative subject under 72 chars, and the body says why.
127|
128|## Design
129|
130|Minimalist, functional, elegant. No generic AI-template look: no purple or violet anywhere, no gradient blobs, no glassmorphism, no emoji icons, no stock hero sections.
131|
132|The palette comes from Meta's brand. Meta blue `#0866FF` is the single accent, `#0064E0` for hover and pressed states. Text is near-black `#1C2B33`. Surfaces are white `#FFFFFF` and soft gray `#F1F4F7`. Dark mode keeps the same accent on a near-black surface: `#0B1215` surface, `#E4E6EB` text.
133|
134|The layout is typography-first. The book sits centered with a comfortable measure, about 60 to 70 chars per line. The companion chat lives in a quiet side panel. Whitespace is generous, the accent color is single, motion is subtle: under 200 ms, and it respects `prefers-reduced-motion`.
135|
136|These values live as CSS custom properties in [app/tokens.css](app/tokens.css), which is the source of truth.

138|## Hooks
139|
140|`npm install` (or `npm run prepare`) points `core.hooksPath` at `.githooks`. The `pre-commit` hook rejects staged files over 5000 tokens and staged secrets. The `prepare-commit-msg` hook adds the co-author trailer. Run the checks by hand with `npm run check:size` and `npm run check:secrets`, and the hook tests with `npm run test:hooks`.

1|# Contracts
2|
3|Music generation must never block the reader. Each module below owns one
4|job and can be swapped without touching the others. Import direction is
5|`core <- server` and `core <- app`. Server and client components never
6|import each other. `app/page.tsx` may import `server/books.ts`. Client
7|files never do.
8|
9|## Book data
10|
11|`data/books/oz/book.json` holds the frozen text: id, title, author,
12|`textVersion` hash, chapters with `start_n` and `end_n`, and paragraphs
13|with `id`, `ch`, `n`, and `text`. `analysis.json` is the scene source
14|the reader consumes: the same scenes plus Jev vectors, the Muse
15|override, and the `final` emotion. `scenes.json` is the pipeline
16|intermediate that `analysis.json` mirrors. The reader consumes the book
17|fields, scene ranges and titles, and the `final` vector with intensity
18|and tempo. It never sees `jev`, `muse_override`, or provenance.
19|`core/reader.ts` defines `buildReaderModel`, which joins paragraphs to
20|scenes by ordinal range and throws on unordered scenes or on paragraphs
21|covered zero or two times. The `resplit` pipeline step (after
22|`classify`, before `cluster`) cuts candidate scenes into ~100 to 160
23|word windows, classifies each window with Jev, and splits at the
24|strongest persistent dominant-emotion shift (auto at margin 0.30,
25|Muse decides 0.15 to 0.30, none below). The first part keeps the
26|scene id with letter-suffixed later parts; provenance lands under
27|`provenance.resplit` in `analysis.json`: one entry per cut (`from`,
28|`at_n`, `margin`, `window_left`/`window_right` from the window means,
29|`final_left`/`final_right` from the re-classified parts,
30|`decided_by`), plus `merged_back` (parts re-classified to the same top
31|emotion and folded back), `rejected` (Muse declined), and
32|`window_failures` (Jev failed, scene left whole) and `muse_failures` (Muse resplit call or titles failed, scene left whole).
33|
34|## Scene reader
35|
36|One static route per scene (`app/leer/[sceneId]`, `dynamicParams`
37|false); `/` redirects to the first scene. The layout mounts the music
38|container once and passes slim metadata for all scenes: id, chapter,
39|and emotion triple only. Each scene page builds its view with
40|`buildSceneView` and ships only that scene's text, its chapter title,
41|and neighbor ids. Sub-pages come from `paginateScene`, which closes a
42|page when the next paragraph would pass 250 words or the line budget
43|(`FIRST_PAGE_LINES` 12 on page one, `LINES_PER_PAGE` 13 after, each
44|paragraph costing `ceil(chars / CHARS_PER_LINE)` lines with
45|`CHARS_PER_LINE` 58). Paragraphs that outlast a page split at a
46|sentence boundary (word fallback); fragments share `n`, later ones
47|carry `cont`, and rejoin exactly. A two-line chapter title
48|(`TITLE_CHARS_PER_LINE` 26) costs every page 2 lines. The pager moves sub-pages in client state and
49|pushes routes with `router.push`, never `<Link>`; going back lands on
50|the previous scene's last sub-page through a one-shot client flag, never
51|a URL param, so prerendered pages stay static. The client never
52|receives other scenes' text, titles, or summaries. One grid holds the
53|top line, image pane, reading column, vault margin, and bottom band;
54|route wrappers use `display: contents`, so music state persists across
55|routes with no portal. The top line reads `LECTORIA`, book and author,
56|then `Chapter N of 24` as a quiet chapter jump (a native select styled
57|as text, options `1. The Cyclone`), then the theme toggle. Each page
58|opens with a kicker `Chapter N`, the chapter title in Newsreader, then
59|muted `Scene k of n` (plus `Page i of m`); no scene name appears
60|anywhere. Book type is 20.5px / 1.7, no paragraph gaps, 1.5em indent,
61|blue drop cap on page one. The body never scrolls at 1280×800; the
62|reading column scrolls inside itself. The word budget stays the upper
63|bound and the line budget keeps every sub-page inside 1280×800 without
64|scroll.
65|
66|## Music library
67|
68|The library is a static `public/music/manifest.json`, version 3, fetched
69|by the client from `/music/manifest.json`. A static file needs no route,
70|ships from the CDN, and swaps by replacing files only. Tracks may be
71|several minutes long and are not loops unless marked so. A version 2
72|manifest migrates inline to one implicit `default` soundtrack of style
73|`orchestral`.
74|
75|`MusicManifest = { version, styles, soundtracks, tracks, playlists }`.
76|`StyleInfo = { id, name }` where `id` is a lowercase slug and `name` is
77|the display name. `Soundtrack = { id, name, style }` plus
78|optional `credit`. `Track = { id, src, title, emotion, vector,
79|intensity, tempo, durationSec, soundtrack, style }` plus optional
80|`startSec` (default 0, where playback starts on first play and on each
81|loop), `endSec` (default the media end, where the track stops or loops),
82|`gainDb` (default 0, a loudness trim in dB, in -24..12),
83|`loop` (default true), `source` (`generated`, `jamendo`, or
84|`recording`), `artist`, `composer`, `license`, `attribution`, and
85|`sourceUrl` (https only). `durationSec` is the playable length: the
86|segment end (or the file end) minus `startSec`. `startSec` and `endSec`
87|are absolute media times with `startSec < endSec`; `endSec` stays within
88|`startSec + durationSec`. The player scales volume by the track gain and
89|ends or loops at `effectiveEnd`, the earlier of `endSec` and the loaded
90|media end. `emotion` is the hand label: one of the 8
91|emotion ids in `core/types.ts`. The vector covers the 8 ids with finite
92|entries in 0..1. Every track names a soundtrack id, every track style
93|matches its soundtrack style, and every style is a listed style id.
94|`core/music.ts` owns `parseManifest`, which rejects unknown versions,
95|duplicate ids, unknown soundtrack or style ids, style mismatches,
96|missing fields, bad vectors, NaN entries, out-of-range numbers,
97|a negative `startSec`, a bad `gainDb` or `endSec`, unknown `source`
98|values, a non-boolean
99|`playlistOnly`, and any `src`
100|that is not a `/music/` path or `https` URL. Unknown fields stay
101|ignored. A soundtrack with no
102|tracks parses. The reader calls it on every fetch, so a bad drop-in
103|fails loudly in dev. Remote audio lives on one Blob store, so
104|`media-src` in `next.config.ts` lists exactly
105|`https://3vuhzq2wmortnuxj.public.blob.vercel-storage.com`. Build the
106|manifest with `npm run build:music data/music/labels.json
107|data/music/library.json --out public/music/manifest.json`, which runs
108|`pipeline/labels-to-manifest.ts` and validates the result before
109|writing.
110|
111|`Track.playlistOnly` defaults to false. A true value marks a playlist
112|only track: it still names a soundtrack and style, but no emotion pick
113|ever returns it. `MusicManifest.playlists` holds
114|`Playlist = { id, label, trackIds }` entries, most notably
115|`just-play-chopin`. A missing key parses as an empty list, and a v2
116|migration gives an empty list. Parse rejects duplicate playlist ids,
117|empty labels, non-array `trackIds`, and any `trackIds` entry that names
118|no track, with the playlist and the id in the message.
119|
120|## Selection
121|
122|`MusicSelection = { style }` is the session: `style` scopes every pick.
123|There is one mode only. Every scheduled select ranges over all tracks in
124|the current style and draws among the tracks with the scene emotion (or
125|the best same-style tracks when the emotion is missing) within
126|`randomTolerance` (0.05) of the best score, keeps the current track when
127|it is eligible, and avoids an immediate repeat otherwise. The style is
128|the user's choice, changed with the style selector. The default style is
129|the first listed style with tracks; a stored style with tracks wins. The
130|session persists `{ style, volume, muted }` in localStorage under
131|`lectoria.music.v1`. Old values with `mode` or `soundtrackId` load by
132|`style` alone and ignore unknown fields; a stored object without
133|`volume` or `muted` loads `volume: null` and `muted: false`. A bad
134|`volume` (not a finite number in 0..1) loads null and the player starts
135|at 0.8; a bad `muted` loads false. A stored style with no tracks falls
136|back to the default. Storage exceptions never break playback. Dwell
137|and min-track rules hold. The core never calls `Math.random`; the
138|reader injects it and tests pass a seeded stub.
139|
140|## Next track and style change
141|
142|`nextTrack` cycles same-emotion tracks in score order across the whole
143|style, wrapping and skipping the current, then the best same-style track
144|overall when the emotion is missing. A null scene cycles the style set
145|in id order. One track or none gives null.
146|
147|`requestStyleChange` picks the best match for the scene in the new style
148|by score. It never crosses styles. The scheduler applies it at once
149|with the normal crossfade and holds the choice like a Next. There is no
150|mix toggle and no soundtrack-change button.
151|
152|## Playlist mode
153|
154|`SchedulerState.playlist` holds `{ id, index }` while a fixed playlist
155|plays. `enterPlaylist` switches at once to the first `trackIds` entry
156|with `crossfadeSec`, no dwell and no min-track rule. While it is on,
157|scene changes update the active scene but never switch, `requestNext`
158|and `noteTrackEnded` advance to the next entry in order and wrap from
159|the last to the first, and playlist tracks run to their end because the
160|player forces looping off. `exitPlaylist` clears the playlist state and
161|switches at once to the best match for the current scene under the
162|restored selection. The playlist is never persisted, so a reload returns
163|to emotion mode. The style selector stays disabled while it is on, and
164|the style list hides styles with only playlist tracks.
165|
166|## Similarity and config
167|
168|`Similarity = (scene, track, weights) => number`, where
169|`SceneSignal = { vector, intensity, tempo }`. The default is
170|`bhattacharyyaSimilarity`: both 8-emotion vectors renormalize to sum 1
171|(an all-zero vector gives an affinity of 0), `E` is the sum of
172|`sqrt(s_k * t_k)`, and the score is `weights.emotion * E` plus
173|`weights.intensity` and `weights.tempo` each for intensity and tempo
174|closeness. Scoring and ranking pass the resolved config weights in, so
175|a weights override changes the ranking. `cosineSimilarity` over
176|`buildFeatures` output stays as an exported alternative. One exported object,
177|`MUSIC_CONFIG`, holds `similarity`, `weights`, `dwellSec` (20),
178|`sceneEntryDwellSec` (5), `minTrackSec` (45), `crossfadeSec` (3), and
179|`randomTolerance` (0.05). Everything else reads from it. Ranking ties go
180|to the lower track id. Route entries use `sceneEntryDwellSec` as the
181|dwell override; scoring and overrides are unchanged. One path scopes,
182|ranks, and draws: `audibleTracks` is the one playlist-only filter,
183|`compareTrackId` the one tie-break, `rankScored` scores each track once
184|(best first, ties to lower id), and `selectScheduled` runs the tolerance
185|window, keep-current, and min-track hold with one rng call per draw.
186|
187|## Music session
188|
189|`core/music-session.ts` is the single policy owner behind the reader.
190|The reader sends intents (`sceneEntered`, `tick`, `skip`, `previous`,
191|`styleChanged`, `trackEnded`, `playlistToggled`) through
192|`startSession` and `dispatch` with explicit `nowSec` and `rng` values,
193|so all timing is testable without timers or a render. `dispatch`
194|returns the same session object when nothing changed, so the 1 s tick
195|rerenders nothing. The reader cues music on scene entry only: one
196|`sceneEntered` per route id, gated by an id comparison, so sub-page
197|moves never reach the session. The session holds the scheduler state,
198|the Previous history, the selection, the fade, and the replay nonce,
199|and derives the view the player renders: track id, fade, nonce,
200|canPrev/canSkip, playlist flag, style.
201|
202|## Selection scheduler
203|
204|`core/music-schedule.ts` is a pure state machine. The session calls
205|`observeScene`, `tickScheduler`, `requestNext`, `noteTrackEnded`,
206|`requestManualTrack`, `switchStyle`, `enterPlaylist`, and
207|`exitPlaylist` with explicit `nowSec` values, so all timing is testable
208|without timers. State holds the current track id and when it started, the active
209|scene id, the pending scene id and since when, and the skip override
210|with the scene it belongs to.
211|
212|A newly entered scene becomes pending and the dwell clock restarts, so
213|fast scrolling keeps only the newest scene. The first track ever plays
214|at once with no dwell. After the pending scene holds for `dwellSec` it
215|becomes active and the override clears. Then a scheduled select draws
216|among the in-style tracks within `randomTolerance` of the best score,
217|keeping the current track when it is eligible, and switches to the
218|drawn track only once the current track played `minTrackSec`. A tick
219|passes the active scene back through the same draw, so a hold from
220|`minTrackSec` releases on time, unless a skip override stands: ticks
221|return no change while it is set, and only a new scene promotion
222|clears it. A switch reports the normal crossfade length (3 s, 0 s for
223|the first track ever). The skip choice holds until the next scene change;
224|after that, dwell and the draw apply with the override track as the
225|current track. A null scene means a failed analysis with no vector, so
226|it never triggers a switch. A non-looping track that ends fades into
227|the best remaining track, excluding the one that ended, and clears the
228|skip override.
229|
230|## Player
231|
232|`app/player.tsx` takes the track, `replayNonce`, the fade length for
233|the latest switch, `canPrev`/`canSkip` with their handlers, volume and
234|mute with their handlers, the style list with the current style and its
235|handler, the end-of-track handler, and the playlist props
236|(`playlistOn`, `playlistLabel`, `onTogglePlaylist`,
237|`controlsDisabled`). It owns two `audio`
238|elements, play state, volume, and the equal-power crossfade
239|(cos/sin gains over the fade time, driven by `requestAnimationFrame`).
240|It never uses the `loop` attribute. Volume lives in a ref, so the slider
241|never re-runs the track effect or touches `src`. A new track request
242|mid-fade cancels the pending fade and fades from the audible element to
243|the newest track. On load each track seeks to `startSec` once metadata
244|is available. Long tracks with `loop` true crossfade into the other
245|element playing the same track from `startSec` when `currentTime`
246|reaches `duration - fade`, where `fade` is the latest scheduler fade
247|length, or the config `crossfadeSec` when none was reported yet. When
248|`loop` is false the player reports the end and the scheduler picks the
249|next-best track excluding the ended one. Pause stops both elements and
250|freezes the fade in place; play resumes the audible elements from the
251|frozen point. Audio starts once, on the first press, with fade 0.
252|Audio starts only after the user presses play. Reduced motion is read in
253|state with a change listener and affects visuals only, never the fade.
254|
255|The bottom band is one row: the pager with book ticks left, the player
256|centre-right. The pager reads `Scene k of n` between `‹` `›` buttons
257|(`Previous page` / `Next page`, arrow keys keep working), above one
258|tick per scene (current in accent) and muted `Scene i of N`. The player
259|holds Previous, Play/Pause, Next, mute (`Mute` / `Unmute`), a `Volume`
260|slider, the now-playing line (ellipsis, full line in `title`), then
261|the stickers and Chopin. The line shows `display title · composer`,
262|then the source artist as a link with an arrow icon when the manifest
263|gives a URL. Orchestra and Piano are sticker buttons
264|(`/art/stickers/violin.svg`, `/art/stickers/piano.svg`, Noto Emoji,
265|Apache-2.0), shown while two styles have tracks, with `aria-pressed`
266|for the selected one, a white die-cut outline, and a Meta-blue dot
267|below it. Previous walks the session history and restarts the track
268|with no history; Next cycles same-emotion tracks in the style.
269|A `Just play Chopin` round image button (`/art/chopin-just-play-me.png`,
270|40 px) appears only when the manifest defines that playlist; while
271|pressed it shows a 2 px Meta-blue ring plus scale 1.05. On manifest
272|failure the band shows `The music is resting. The book is all yours.`
273|Motion stays under 200 ms, except the image hover expand at 260 ms.
274|`app/player.tsx` keeps the audio engine, transport, and band layout;
275|`app/player-controls.tsx` holds the stickers and playlist toggle;
276|`app/music-prefs.ts` owns storage. The heading keeps
277|`:focus:not(:focus-visible){outline:none}`. No user-visible emotion
278|labels exist; ids stay as they are. `core/music-credit.ts` builds the
279|line as a pure function with tests. `core/music-history.ts` is the
280|bounded history stack; `requestManualTrack` holds a manual pick.
281|
282|## Image api
283|
284|`POST /api/images` (Node runtime, `maxDuration` 120). Request is a
285|discriminated union: `{ kind: "passage", bookId, textVersion, n }` names
286|the paragraph where the selection starts, `{ kind: "scene", bookId,
287|textVersion, sceneId }` names the scene. Validation is strict: known
288|book, matching `textVersion`, integer `n` inside the book, known
289|`sceneId`. Any other body is a 400 with a generic English message.
290|The client sends ordinals and ids only, never text. "Illustrate
291|scene" uses the scene id from the route.
292|
293|Responses (typed in `core/types.ts`): `{ status: "ready", url, cached,
294|caption }` with a Vercel Blob URL, never bytes; `{ status: "pending" }`
295|when another request holds the lock, so the client reposts
296|every 3 s up to ~2 minutes; `{ status: "error", code, message }`
297|where code is `quota`, `budget`, `daily_budget`, `unavailable`, or
298|`bad_request` with a friendly English message. Both `budget` and
299|`daily_budget` answer `MSG_CREDITS_OUT` (`core/images.ts`): the free
300|credits ran out, bring your own key, and meanwhile the Oz reader is
301|ready with its soundtrack and illustrations. It never says "come back
302|tomorrow". The UI links the Oz sentence via `CREDITS_OUT_LIBRARY_HREF`
303|(`"/"`). Caption is the scene title, or the paragraph's first words,
304|built server-side.
305|
306|The passage cache key is book plus start paragraph plus `textVersion`
307|plus `PROMPT_VERSION` (`v1`); the scene key swaps in the scene id.
308|Both map to a deterministic Blob path (`addRandomSuffix: false`,
309|`allowOverwrite: false`). An Upstash Redis index maps key to Blob URL,
310|so hits are one GET; on an index miss the server lists by path prefix
311|before generating and backfills the index.
312|Quota is 5 new images per person per day by hashed IP and signed
313|cookie, whichever runs out first; a shared spend counter in integer
314|micro-dollars sits under `SPEND_CAP_USD` (default 10), plus a daily
315|counter per UTC day under `DAILY_SPEND_CAP_USD` (default 2, 48 h key
316|TTL). Failures refund quota and both counters and release the lock.
317|Both caps apply only to requests paid with our key; a future
318|bring-your-own-key path skips them. Free uploads allow one book per
319|person (`FREE_BOOKS_PER_PERSON` = 1, hashed IP plus anon cookie, no
320|day, ~10-day TTL; `checkBookQuota`/`refundBookQuota` in
321|`server/images/quota.ts`, no route yet).
322|
323|## Picture vault and style pref
324|
325|The pane shows the scene picture behind a `Picture this scene` pill on
326|a paper-grain placeholder (`Sketching…` while loading, retry on
327|error). The image fills the pane, expands on a 250 ms hover (max 72vw
328|by 78vh), and opens the shared lightbox on click. `Picture this` pops
329|8 px above a 3+ char selection and inserts one figure after the
330|selection end paragraph (`pickEndN` over ordinals), captioned with the
331|selected text. Figures persist per scene in client memory, one request
332|at a time. The vault lists the scene picture first, then figures in
333|text order, each with jump-to-figure pulse and expand; the style picker
334|below stores `{ kind: "preset", id } | { kind: "custom", text }` in
335|`lectoria.imageStyle`. The style is UI only: `requestStyleFields` in
336|`app/image-style.ts` returns `{}` until the `/api/images` style
337|contract lands, and request bodies spread its result. The credit stays
338|`In the style of W. W. Denslow` until the adapter sends a style. The
339|developer view (Shift+D or `?dev`, hidden otherwise) shows emotion
340|bars, intensity, tempo, and track from data the reader holds. Theme
341|persists in `lectoria.theme`; fonts are Newsreader and Instrument Sans
342|via `next/font/google`.
343|
344|## Chat api
345|
346|Contract only, no routes. Request `{ bookId, textVersion, positionN,
347|spoilerMode, messages }` carries the chat history and the reader
348|position. The response is streamed text. The server builds context from
349|the book text up to `positionN`, or the whole book when `spoilerMode` is
350|on, with the book prefix first and the question last so readers share
351|the prompt cache. The system prompt answers only from that text and
352|refuses the rest. Types live in `core/types.ts`.
353|
354|## Quotas and budget
355|
356|Server only. Spend is counted in integer micro-dollars: reserve with
357|Redis `INCRBY` before each model call, refund with `DECRBY` after, one
358|reserve per call including retries. The server clamps every model tool
359|argument. Clients never see keys or raw errors. Generic messages go to
360|the client, details stay in server logs.

284|`POST /api/images` (Node runtime, `maxDuration` 120). Request is a
285|discriminated union: `{ kind: "passage", bookId, textVersion, n }` names

287|textVersion, sceneId }` names the scene. Validation is strict: known

289|`sceneId`. Any other body is a 400 with a generic English message.

291|scene" uses the scene id from the route.
